description: Brali Research Watch review batch for 2026-09-15. The pass searched for practical learning mechanisms not already represented in the current canonical Growth Library or protocol override layer. Two 2025 meta-analyses support genuinely distinct low-risk learning protocols: prequestions for targeted information before learning, and self-explanation for generating and checking understanding during digital learning. A micro-break candidate was explicitly rejected as a new page because Brali already has a reviewed micro-break evidence boundary attached to the existing Pomodoro-style protocol.

research_candidates.title: The Effect of Prequestions on Learning: A Multilevel Meta-Analysis
research_candidates.review_notes: Multilevel meta-analysis reports a clear benefit for information targeted by prequestions (g = 0.66) and essentially no general benefit for non-prequestioned information (g = 0.01). Conditions combining feedback with prequestions showed stronger targeted learning than prequestions alone. Publish only as a targeting protocol: ask specific questions, attempt an answer, learn, and check. Do not claim broad lesson-wide improvement, a magic question count, or guaranteed benefit for every learner.

research_candidates.title: Enhancing Academic Performance Through Self-Explanation in Digital Learning Environments (DLEs): A Three-Level Meta-Analysis
research_candidates.review_notes: Three-level meta-analysis of 204 effect sizes from 56 studies in digital learning environments reports an overall positive effect on academic performance (g = 0.46), with positive retention and transfer effects and moderation by pacing and knowledge type. Publish a bounded generate-check-correct protocol. Do not claim one best modality, prompt, frequency, or universal effect outside the reviewed digital-learning context.

evidence_decisions.source_title: The Effect of Prequestions on Learning: A Multilevel Meta-Analysis
evidence_decisions.citation_text: King-Shepard QW, Walker J, Nokes-Malach TJ, Carpenter SK, Fraundorf SH. Educational Psychology Review. 2025;37:115.
evidence_decisions.study_design: Multilevel meta-analysis of the prequestion literature examining learning of prequestioned and non-prequestioned content across variations in learning event, participant sample, and assessment conditions.
evidence_decisions.population: Learners represented across the studies included in the meta-analysis; the practical protocol is intentionally population-neutral and does not convert subgroup findings into a universal dose.
evidence_decisions.intervention_or_exposure: Questions attempted before an educational activity, compared with conditions without those prequestions; some study conditions also provided feedback.
evidence_decisions.supported_claim: Prequestions can improve later learning of the specific information they target. The meta-analysis reported g = 0.66 for prequestioned information and g = 0.01 for non-prequestioned information; feedback alongside prequestions was associated with stronger targeted learning.
unsupported_or_overstated_claims: Prequestions improve learning of the entire lesson.
Any question asked before learning will be beneficial.
There is one evidence-backed optimal number of prequestions.
A wrong first answer is itself sufficient without later exposure or correction.
Prequestions replace retrieval practice, practice problems, or feedback after learning.
limitations: The average benefit is specific to prequestioned information rather than a broad benefit to all content.
The meta-analysis does not establish one universal question count, timing rule, or content format.
Effect sizes summarize heterogeneous studies and do not guarantee the same result for an individual learning session.
evidence_decisions.notes: Editorial action: publish a new Skill Sprint protocol because no prequestion/pretesting surface was found in the canonical index or override layer. Make the target-versus-nontarget boundary prominent.

evidence_decisions.source_title: Enhancing Academic Performance Through Self-Explanation in Digital Learning Environments (DLEs): A Three-Level Meta-Analysis
evidence_decisions.citation_text: Tan LP, Gong SY, Wang YJ, Guo XR, Xu XZ, Wang YQ. Educational Psychology Review. 2025;37:20.
evidence_decisions.study_design: Three-level meta-analysis of 204 effect sizes extracted from 56 studies comparing self-explanation with no-self-explanation conditions in digital learning environments.
evidence_decisions.population: Learners in digital learning environments across the included studies. Effects varied with learning-environment and material characteristics.
evidence_decisions.intervention_or_exposure: Self-explanation prompts or activities during digital learning, compared with conditions without self-explanation.
evidence_decisions.supported_claim: Self-explanation in digital learning environments had a positive average effect on academic performance (reported g = 0.46), with positive average effects for retention and transfer. Effects were moderated by pacing and knowledge type, with larger effects reported for learner-centered pacing and conceptual or mixed knowledge than for procedural knowledge.
unsupported_or_overstated_claims: Self-explanation is always better than other learning strategies.
One explanation prompt or modality is universally optimal.
The average effect applies unchanged outside digital learning environments.
A fluent explanation is accurate without checking it against the source.
limitations: The reviewed evidence is specifically about digital learning environments.
The meta-analysis reports heterogeneity and moderation rather than a uniform effect across all settings.
The authors identify the quality and standardization of self-explanations as areas needing further research.
evidence_decisions.notes: Editorial action: publish a new Skill Sprint protocol built around generate -> inspect gap -> source check -> correct. Preserve digital-learning scope and moderation rather than presenting self-explanation as a universal study rule.

summary.duplicate_note: A new micro-break page was not created because Brali already has review-registry-pomodoro-microbreak-evidence-boundary.json linked to the existing 25-minute-pomodoro-focus-sprints protocol.
summary.safety: Both published protocols are low-risk educational practices. No medical, financial, or mental-health treatment claim is introduced.
